name: Democratic Republic of Vietnam
info: The communist state proclaimed by Hồ Chí Minh in Hanoi in 1945, which defeated France at Điện Biên Phủ, ruled the North after the partition of 1954 and conquered the South in 1975.

facts.founder: Hồ Chí Minh, who declared independence on 2 September 1945 during the August Revolution
facts.predecessor: Empire of Vietnam and the Nguyễn dynasty; French Indochina, under Japanese occupation from 1940
facts.successor: Socialist Republic of Vietnam (2 July 1976), formed with the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam

t: Hồ Chí Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945; the Viet Minh, aided by Chinese communists from 1949, defeated the French at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu in 1954, and the Geneva Accords left it the zone north of the 17th parallel.

Its land reform of 1953–1956 gave land to poor and landless peasants but was carried out with violence; estimates of the executions range from a few thousand to far higher, and Hồ Chí Minh apologised for its errors on 18 August 1956.

Under Lê Duẩn from 1960 it waged war on the Republic of Vietnam through the Viet Cong and the Ho Chi Minh trail, and after the fall of Saigon in 1975 the two halves were reunited as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam in 1976.
dyk: A Politburo document dated 4 May 1953 fixed the planned executions of the land reform "in principle at the ratio of one per one thousand people of the total population".
ev: After Japan's surrender the Việt Minh enter Hanoi in the August Revolution, and Hồ Chí Minh proclaims the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September
The National Assembly adopts the first constitution in November, and in December the First Indochina War begins as the French reoccupy Hanoi
The Viet Minh Land Reform Law of 4 December opens the land reform, carried out until 1956
The Viet Minh defeat the French at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu, and the Geneva Accords divide Vietnam provisionally along the 17th parallel
Hồ Chí Minh apologises on 18 August for the errors of the land reform, and rioting against its excesses breaks out in a largely Catholic district in November
Lê Duẩn's leadership begins, and the North goes to war with the Republic of Vietnam through its proxy the Viet Cong
Saigon falls on 30 April, and South Vietnam comes under the Provisional Revolutionary Government
North and South Vietnam are officially reunited on 2 July as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam

sections.foundation:
After the Japanese invasion of French Indochina in 1940, the communist revolutionary Hồ Chí Minh established the Việt Minh Front in 1941 to resist the occupation and win independence; cloaked in nationalism, it was designed to appeal to a wider population than the Indochinese Communist Party could command. Soon after Japan surrendered, the Việt Minh entered Hanoi in the August Revolution, and on 2 September 1945 Hồ Chí Minh declared the independence of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam, replacing the Nguyễn dynasty.

The new state claimed all of Vietnam, but much of the South was not aligned with it. British troops arrived in Saigon on 12 September 1945 and French troops took over public buildings there, while in the north the Chinese Nationalist Army came to disarm the Japanese and forced the Việt Minh to accommodate Kuomintang-supported nationalists. An election held mainly in the North in January 1946 produced a National Assembly whose party makeup was decided before the vote. The Franco-Chinese and Ho–Sainteny Agreements of March 1946 let French forces replace the Chinese north of the 16th parallel, and the Chinese troops left Haiphong in June.
sections.socioeconomy:
Land reform was central to the state's programme. The Land Reform Law of 4 December 1953 provided for confiscating the land of landlords judged enemies of the regime, requisitioning it from others and buying it with bonds. Carried out from 1953 to 1956, it affected more than 4 million rural people, and rent reduction nearly 8 million; most land was given out without payment, with priority for Viet Minh fighters and their families. It was carried out with violence against landowners identified, sometimes incorrectly, as landlords. Estimates of those executed range up to 200,000; Gareth Porter put the figure between 800 and 2,500, Edwin E. Moise at about 5,000 and later 13,500, and Vo Nhan Tri found a party document naming 15,000 wrongful executions. Over 12,000 people died of famine in Viet Minh zones by the end of 1954.

The aim was collective farming. After a Three Year Plan (1957–1960), agricultural production reached 5.4 million tonnes, over double the levels before the Indochina War, and by 1960 there were 40,000 cooperatives on nearly nine-tenths of all farmland. By 1961, 86 percent of farmers belonged to low-level cooperatives, and by 1971 the great majority were in high-level cooperatives without individual ownership of land.
sections.military:
During the First Indochina War (1946–54) the Viet Minh controlled most rural areas while many towns fell to the French. Chinese communist forces reached the border in 1949, and Chinese aid transformed the Viet Minh from a guerrilla militia into a standing army; with that help Võ Nguyên Giáp built a modern army that defeated the French at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu in 1954. Before that, in the summer of 1946, the Viet Minh colluded with French forces to eliminate Vietnamese nationalists: about 13,000 were reported destroyed in Tonkin, and another estimate gives 15,000 massacred across northern Vietnam.

From 1960 the North made war on the Republic of Vietnam through the Viet Cong, sending troops and supplies down the Ho Chi Minh trail, and in 1962 it intensified the infiltration of men and materiel, while Beijing supplied the Viet Cong with small arms and heavier weapons. China, the DPRK and the Soviet Union gave aid and troops; against them the United States, Australia, the Republic of Korea, Thailand and New Zealand supported the South. North Vietnam also sent troops to fight beside the Pathet Lao in the Laotian Civil War and the Khmer Rouge in the Cambodian Civil War. After the United States withdrew by 1973, the South was swiftly overrun.
sections.governance:
North Vietnam was a unitary and centralised Marxist–Leninist state with a constitution modelled on Joseph Stalin's 1936 Constitution of the Soviet Union; its first constitution was adopted by the National Assembly in November 1946. Hồ Chí Minh led it from 1945 to 1960 and Lê Duẩn from 1960 to 1976. In its first years the Viet Minh consolidated power by terrorising and purging rival nationalist groups and Trotskyist activists, and after the Chinese withdrawal Võ Nguyên Giáp moved to secure a monopoly of power. In 1948 the state took what has been called an irreversible proletarian turn: the Indochinese Communist Party, whose membership rose from 5,000 in late 1945 to about 180,000 by the end of 1948, resolved to eradicate judicial independence and ran rectification campaigns to indoctrinate party members, soldiers and officials.

The country was divided into provinces, autonomous regions and centrally run cities. The autonomous regions, based on those of China, gave tribal minorities self-government in exchange for accepting Hanoi's control: the Thái-Mèo Autonomous Region from 1955, the Việt Bắc Autonomous Region from 1956 and the Lào-Hà-Yên Autonomous Region from 1957. The "correction of errors" of 1956 ended the land reform, and as many as 23,748 political prisoners were released by September 1957.
sections.impact:
The radicalisation of the state provoked large-scale defections from the maquis to areas held by the French and the State of Vietnam, among them intellectuals, landlords, soldiers and cadres such as Phạm Duy and Nguyễn Văn Thiệu. After the partition of 1954 more than one million northerners went South, including an estimated 60% of the north's one million Catholics, while approximately 100,000 Viet Minh fighters and between 14,000 and 45,000 civilians moved north.

A member of the Eastern Bloc, North Vietnam was recognised by almost all communist countries, China first, and received their aid; many non-aligned states gave it de facto recognition, and its clandestine weapon transfers during the Algerian War made relations with Algeria close. In 1969 Sweden became the first Western country to extend full diplomatic recognition, by December 1972 49 countries had relations with it, and 96 did so during its existence. Japan agreed relations in September 1973 and, after North Vietnamese demands for reparations, provided an endowment of 13.5 billion yen. The insurgencies it aided in Laos and Cambodia brought the Pathet Lao and the Khmer Rouge to power in 1975.
sections.decline:
The Democratic Republic of Vietnam ended in victory rather than collapse. The United States and its allies withdrew from the war by 1973, and on 30 April 1975 Saigon fell. For the next year the Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam, alongside the North Vietnamese Army, governed the South, though it was seen as a vassal government of North Vietnam. On 2 July 1976 North and South were officially reunited as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, whose government was dominated by holdovers from the North and which adopted the North Vietnamese constitution, flag and anthem.

The unified state kept a Soviet style of socialism as the basis of its political and economic systems and its memberships in Eastern Bloc organisations such as COMECON until the Đổi Mới economic reforms of 1986 and the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991. It went through economic decline and refugee crises and fought the Khmer Rouge in 1978 and China in 1979. The autonomous regions of the North were not continued and were fully abolished by 1978, and the collective farms were abandoned gradually in the 1980s and 1990s.

summary: The Democratic Republic of Vietnam was the communist state founded by Hồ Chí Minh in 1945. It won the First Indochina War, ruled the North after 1954 under a constitution modelled on Stalin's, a violent land reform and collective farms, and through the Vietnam War brought the South under its control in 1975 before merging with it in 1976.
references: Arthur J. Dommen, The Indochinese Experience of the French and the Americans: Nationalism and Communism in Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam (Indiana University Press, 2001)
Michael G. Kort, The Vietnam War Reexamined (Cambridge University Press, 2017)
Nu-Anh Tran, Disunion: Anticommunist Nationalism and the Making of the Republic of Vietnam (University of Hawaiʻi Press, 2022)
Christopher Goscha, Vietnam: A New History (Basic Books, 2016)

pointDescs.1945: The Việt Minh enter Hanoi in the August Revolution, and Hồ Chí Minh proclaims the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September.
pointDescs.1946: French forces replace the Chinese in the north, the first constitution is adopted, and the First Indochina War begins in December.
pointDescs.1948: The state takes a radical turn towards communist revolution as the Indochinese Communist Party grows to about 180,000 members.
pointDescs.1950: Chinese aid, arriving since 1949, turns the Viet Minh into a standing army, and China and the Soviet Union recognise the DRV.
pointDescs.1954: Victory at the Battle of Dien Bien Phu and the Geneva Accords leave the DRV in control of the zone north of the 17th parallel.
pointDescs.1956: The land reform ends in a "correction of errors", Hồ Chí Minh apologises, and riots break out against its excesses.
pointDescs.1960: Lê Duẩn takes the leadership, 40,000 cooperatives cover nearly nine-tenths of the farmland, and war on the South begins through the Viet Cong.
pointDescs.1962: The North intensifies its infiltration of military personnel and materiel into South Vietnam.
pointDescs.1969: Sweden becomes the first Western country to extend full diplomatic recognition to North Vietnam.
pointDescs.1972: By December, 49 countries have established diplomatic relations with North Vietnam.
pointDescs.1973: The United States and its allies withdraw from the war, and Japan agrees to establish diplomatic relations.
pointDescs.1975: Saigon falls on 30 April, and the South comes under the Provisional Revolutionary Government.
pointDescs.1976: North and South are reunited on 2 July as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, which adopts the North's constitution, flag and anthem.

notes: The article names no capital in so many words; Hanoi is where the republic was proclaimed and the seat the article refers to ('Hanoi's control', the embassy in Hanoi).

The article's military section is empty; the military section draws on its history and foreign-relations sections. It gives no dated events for 1963-1972 beyond 1962 and the diplomatic counts, so the curve is thin there.

Execution figures of the land reform are given as the article attributes them (Porter, Moise, Vo Nhan Tri; the 200,000 upper estimate called propaganda by other scholarship). The Szalontai figures (1,337 executed by December 1955) were left out for length.
The article dates the US combat deployment to 1964 in one place; left out.
Reference 'Vu, Tuong (2009)' is a journal article and was left out of references; 'Tran' and 'Goscha' are cited by the article.
